title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Atomic MathReasoner improves mathematical reasoning by selecting a problem-specific composition of specialized atomic-skill experts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A lightweight router enables adaptive use of LoRA experts without costly online composition optimization.
method: Train capability-specific LoRA experts and discover composition prototypes through gradient-free optimization on held-out validation subsets.
Score prototypes using reference-solution token-level negative log-likelihood and filter ambiguous assignments with a confidence margin.

infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond AtomicMath and the offline cost of expert training and prototype discovery are not established by the abstract.

title: The Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift from the Perspective of Natural Science and Engineering Practice
authors: Shengchang Chen
abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, fundamentally driven by the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm, rely on setting external objectives and iterative trial-and-error. When confronted with complex nonlinear problems containing noise and conflicting constraints, this paradigm inherently induces statistical smoothing and compromise, yielding black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology, reconstructing the solving process into four irreversible stages: Deconstruction, Structure, Construction, and Solving. The method suspends a priori presuppositions to strip unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants inherent to the problem, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to these invariants, and executes the mapping directly to generate the solution. Evaluation metrics and experience are relegated to a posteriori verification. Demonstrated through cross-disciplinary practices including number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, this methodology transcends the statistical fitting bottleneck. Structure-Driven and Objective-Driven methodologies are complementary: when structure is sufficient, solutions are directly constructed; when lacking, it degenerates into the OD path.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes replacing objective-led trial and error with invariant-based solution construction when sufficient problem structure is available.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For nonlinear engineering problems, the framework aims to enable interpretable, directly constructed solutions rather than statistical compromises.
method: Deconstruction: suspend prior assumptions and disentangle coupled units.
Structure: extract rigid invariants intrinsic to the problem.
Construction → Solving: build invariant-anchored equivalent mappings, execute them, and verify results afterward.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites demonstrations in number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, but reports no quantitative benchmarks or evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Practical value depends on identifying sufficient invariants and valid equivalent mappings; when structure is insufficient, the framework falls back to objective-driven optimization.
infographic.paper_title: The Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift from the Perspective of Natural Science and Engineering Practice

title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
authors: Hai Wang, Bretislav Hajek, Chonghe Jiang, Minwei Kong, Ao Qu, Huatian Gong
abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.

infographic.key_insight: The FrontierOR Challenge tests whether LLM agents can design scalable optimization algorithms across diverse operations research problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Successful agentic workflows could reduce the specialist effort needed to develop routing, scheduling, and network design algorithms.

infographic.paper_title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research

title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
authors: Ahmad AliAhmad, Khemraj Shukla
abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

infographic.key_insight: PINN training can match full-space optimization within a small Hessian-eigenvector subspace selected by gradient alignment rather than curvature magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gradient-aligned subspaces offer a foundation for optimizers tailored to the ill-conditioned loss landscapes of physics-informed PDE solvers.
method: Compute a full Hessian eigendecomposition.
Select the dominant aligned subspace (DAS) by gradient alignment, not eigenvalue magnitude.

infographic.watch_item: Full Hessian eigendecomposition is costly at scale, and the abstract does not establish end-to-end computational savings.
infographic.paper_title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$

title: PWLNet: A Framework for Linearized Neural Surrogates in Nonlinear Process Optimization
authors: Sunoy Sanyal, Canberk Demir, Metin Türkay, Erdal Aydın
abstract: Neural networks represent nonlinear process systems accurately, but embedding them in optimization is difficult because smooth activations introduce nonlinear, nonconvex constraints. PWLNet is a Python framework for building optimization-compatible neural surrogates through exact and piecewise-linear reformulations. It combines baseline and physics-informed training, optimization-aware pruning, and Pyomo embeddings based on ReLU mixed-integer linear models, exact tanh nonlinear models, PWL-tanh formulations, and binary-free SOSX branch-and-LP. PWL-native training uses the same activation in training and embedding, avoiding extra linearization error. It is evaluated on Boston housing, the Williams-Otto process, the Van de Vusse reactor, and a hydroformylation semi-batch reactor. On Boston housing, SOSX training gave the best common-architecture model (test MAE 1.984, R2 = 0.925). On Williams-Otto, pruning 15% of hidden neurons reduced MILP solution time 6.5-fold while preserving the selected operating point. For the Van de Vusse reactor, a physics-informed ReLU RNN pruned from 32 to 12 hidden units enabled tractable exact MILP embedding and a 4% true-plant economic gain over the best ramp-and-hold policy, while terminal-aware shrinking-horizon prediction reached 99.7% of the direct-shooting reference. For the hydroformylation reactor, one-step exact-tanh IPOPT reached 99.2% of the certified reference product with peak pressure 20.002 bar (limit 20 bar) and 14.36 s total solve time over 280 moves; ReLU and PWL-native controllers achieved comparable recovery, with ReLU fastest. Longer horizons and physics-informed training did not consistently improve closed-loop results. Overall, compact linearized neural surrogates enable accurate, tractable optimization in steady-state and dynamic applications, with constraint fidelity identified as a key direction for improvement.

infographic.key_insight: PWLNet makes neural process surrogates easier to optimize by combining compact networks with exact or piecewise-linear formulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can embed learned steady-state and dynamic process models in Pyomo optimization while balancing predictive accuracy, solve time, and constraint fidelity.

title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
authors: Bjørn André Aaslund, Johannes Berge, Ayoub Haida, Ying Ni, Rita Pimentel
abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

infographic.key_insight: X Hedging replaces neural-network hedging policies with LightGBM tree ensembles, targeting comparable performance with greater efficiency and explainability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a potentially lighter, more interpretable alternative for dynamic option hedging, especially when training data are scarce.

title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
authors: Myeong-Su Lee
abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Integral constraints can improve PINN accuracy by restoring uniform control over error components that the standard loss controls weakly in certain PDE parameter regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Stability analysis can help identify when adding integrated governing equations to a PINN loss is likely to improve solution accuracy.
method: Derive stability estimates for several PDEs with and without integral constraints.
Compare how the losses control specific error components across parameter regimes.
Test the predicted accuracy differences in numerical experiments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments show clear accuracy differences where standard-loss control is predicted to be weak, but similar accuracy where it remains sufficient.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on the PDE and parameter regime; integral constraints are not a universal accuracy improvement.
infographic.paper_title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?

title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
authors: Hongnian Huang, Andrew Stump
abstract: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

infographic.key_insight: On a fixed compact manifold, parallel transport convolution is continuous in L² under C² perturbations of the Riemannian metric, subject to the paper’s localization and transport-path conventions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a theoretical robustness foundation for geometric deep-learning operators when the underlying metric changes slightly.
method: Estimate metric-induced changes in geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a qualitative stability theorem for continuous signals and continuous reference kernels with sufficiently small normal-neighborhood support, not empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The result gives no explicit robustness rate and relies on localization and transport-path conventions that implementations must respect.
infographic.paper_title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations

title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution
authors: Yuhang Li, Gang Wu
abstract: Trace-ratio optimization problems from high-dimensional tensor data appear across numerous research domains including machine learning, signal processing, as well as pattern recognition. Up to now, analytical closed-form expressions remain unavailable for tensor trace-ratio tasks; prevailing techniques mostly adopt inner-outer iterative schemes to tackle such optimization tasks. However, when dealing with high-dimensional tensor data sets, existing multilinear discriminant analysis methods often encounter limitations such as heavy computational costs, insufficient memory space, and interference from redundant features. This paper yields two core contributions.First, we present a closed-form solution under the full row rank condition, and construct a randomized solver targeting large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization. In contrast to prior approaches, the devised algorithm achieves substantial computational speedup.Its core mechanism is to reformulate the original large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization into a tensor least-squares formulation, instead of the much more complicated (generalized) tensor eigenproblems. We derive theoretical error-bound results which verify the reliability of the newly developed algorithm. Second, we build a sparse multilinear discriminant analysis model leveraging the above closed-form result combined with tensor \ell_{2,0}-norm regularization, and propose a sparse multilinear discriminant method for tensor feature selection. The sparse method can identify key discriminative features from high-dimensional data and suppress redundant information. Comprehensive numerical evaluations are conducted over multiple publicly available real-world benchmarks.The proposed methods demonstrate significant advantages in computational efficiency and scalability for large-scale problems, while achieving competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.

infographic.key_insight: A closed-form solution under a full-row-rank condition enables randomized tensor trace-ratio optimization through tensor least squares rather than generalized tensor eigenproblems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets computational and memory bottlenecks in high-dimensional tensor analysis while enabling selection of discriminative features.
method: Derive a closed-form tensor trace-ratio solution under full row rank.
Build a randomized tensor least-squares solver with theoretical error bounds.

infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on multiple public real-world benchmarks report substantial efficiency and scalability advantages, with competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The closed-form result requires full row rank; applicability when this condition fails needs verification.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
authors: Sergei Iudin, Mikhail Podobrii, Dmitry Zheltkov, Stanislav Moiseev
abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

infographic.key_insight: U(1)-symmetric Tensor Trains combine hard-constraint handling with richer representations and diversity-aware sampling to balance exploration and exploitation in combinatorial optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical approach to constrained discrete search when feasible solutions are scarce and objective structure is unknown.
method: Encode hard linear constraints using U(1)-symmetric Tensor Trains.
Enhance the expressibility of sparse symmetric tensors.
Use a graph-based diversity measure to guide training-sample selection.

infographic.paper_title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains

title: Stochastic counterpart of Nesterov's method for sampling and provable non-acceleration of samplers with heavy-ball structure
authors: A. Sharma
abstract: Polyak's heavy-ball method and Nesterov's method are two momentum-based methods that have inspired many optimization techniques used in applied fields, including machine learning. Momentum also provides a connection with sampling, and interestingly, many kinetic Langevin samplers reduce to the heavy-ball recurrence when velocity is eliminated and noise is removed. This observation motivates a natural question: what is the corresponding sampler for Nesterov's method? We propose a sampler whose deterministic part is exactly Nesterov's recurrence, driven by temporally correlated Gaussian noise and requires one new gradient evaluation per step. Noise correlation provides $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ bias for smooth observables. We establish geometric ergodicity for possibly non-convex potentials. For strongly convex potentials with Lipschitz continuous gradients, we obtain contraction rates and show that, up to an additive constant, the energy decays at a rate of order $κ^{-1/2}$, where $κ$ is the condition number. For Gaussian targets, we show that relaxation has square-root dependence on $κ$. We further prove that any sampler based on heavy-ball dynamics with additive noise cannot achieve accelerated convergence uniformly over the class of strongly convex functions. Finally, we compare the proposed sampler with OBABO, BAOAB, HMC, MALA, BPS, and NUTS in numerical experiments and demonstrate the better performance of proposed sampler.

infographic.key_insight: A sampler with exact Nesterov deterministic dynamics and correlated Gaussian noise achieves accelerated relaxation for Gaussian targets, while additive-noise heavy-ball samplers cannot accelerate uniformly over strongly convex functions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a momentum-based sampling option requiring one new gradient evaluation per step, potentially improving efficiency for suitable target distributions.
method: Combine Nesterov's recurrence with temporally correlated Gaussian noise.
Obtain O(h²) bias for smooth observables and prove geometric ergodicity under stated conditions, including possibly non-convex potentials.
Establish order-κ⁻¹ᐟ² energy decay up to an additive constant for strongly convex potentials with Lipschitz gradients.

infographic.watch_item: Accelerated Gaussian relaxation and energy decay do not establish uniformly accelerated sampling for general non-convex targets.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic counterpart of Nesterov's method for sampling and provable non-acceleration of samplers with heavy-ball structure

title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
authors: Mengxiao Gao, Elly K. H. Hung, Yuchen Wu, Yi Yu
abstract: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

infographic.key_insight: A differentially private score estimator achieves nearly matching minimax error bounds, characterizing the privacy–accuracy trade-off and enabling private diffusion modeling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The resulting diffusion model has a privacy guarantee independent of its number of denoising steps and nearly minimax-optimal expected total variation error with appropriate discretization.
method: Represent scores using quadratic B-splines and sample via the exponential mechanism.
Implement private estimation with projected Langevin Monte Carlo in runtime polynomial in sample size.

infographic.paper_title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu
abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

infographic.key_insight: CurvDelta confines model updates to a low-curvature space to learn or forget targeted capabilities while limiting degradation of general capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a preservation-aware approach to LLM adaptation, with CurvLoRA providing a low-rank option designed for greater efficiency.
method: Analyze local preservation-loss geometry around the pre-adaptation model.
Use K-FAC and factorized projection to construct low-curvature updates at LLM scale.
Apply CurvDelta or its low-rank variant, CurvLoRA, to capability learning and selective unlearning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and TOFU/MUSE unlearning report improved acquisition–retention or forgetting–retention trade-offs, with unlearning retention close to from-scratch retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Preservation relies on local, approximate curvature; the abstract does not establish how well it holds for large updates or distribution shifts.
infographic.paper_title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning

title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
authors: Zhouxing Luo, Lei Wang, Xin Liu
abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

infographic.key_insight: Infinity-Wasserstein robust PCA admits an exact finite-dimensional reformulation while retaining samplewise residual information that can reshape the learned principal subspace.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a principled way to make dimensionality reduction more resilient to distributional uncertainty in representation-learning pipelines.
method: Formulate PCA with an infinity-Wasserstein distributional uncertainty set and explicitly construct a worst-case distribution.
Establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee assuming the true distribution has a finite fourth moment.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments supporting computational efficiency and downstream effectiveness, but provides no datasets, metrics, or quantitative gains.
infographic.watch_item: The optimization remains nonconvex, so convergence analysis should not be interpreted as a guarantee of finding a global optimum.
infographic.paper_title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm

title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
authors: Leevan Ling, Shu Ma, Yizhong Sun
abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.

infographic.key_insight: Neural approximation power alone cannot ensure PINN convergence: discrete residuals must control continuous error within stable admissible trial classes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For linear elliptic Dirichlet PDEs, the framework guides collocation-point requirements and scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weighting.
method: Extend kernel collocation theory using elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency.
Identify admissible neural subclasses whose continuous residuals are controlled by discrete loss.
Construct admissible tanh-MLP comparison networks to establish constrained convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence results, including conditional unconstrained convergence under joint network and sampling refinement, but no numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Unconstrained PINN convergence remains conditional; expressive networks alone do not guarantee the required stability and consistency.
infographic.paper_title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks

title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
authors: Uzma Shafiq, Matthew England, Nayyar Zaidi
abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning can improve computer algebra by guiding costly symbolic algorithms or performing symbolic computations directly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ML-guided algorithm selection and heuristics could reduce computational costs in symbolic workflows used for scientific and engineering analysis.
method: Systematically review ML applications in computer algebra.
Compare approaches ranging from decision trees to transformers.
Cover cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner bases, symbolic integration, and other tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a literature synthesis rather than new performance results and identifies missing benchmark datasets as a barrier to reliable comparison.
infographic.watch_item: Limited benchmarks hinder assessment of model generalizability; symbolic outputs also require mathematical verification.
infographic.paper_title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra

title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
authors: Morteza Kimiaei, Saman Babaie--Kafaki
abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

infographic.key_insight: Safeguarded online learning can improve nonlinear conjugate gradient robustness while preserving its classical two-term, low-storage structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach is promising for PDE-constrained optimization where function and gradient evaluations are expensive.
method: Use two independent online extreme learning machines to predict recovery coefficients and bounded step-size corrections.
Accept predictions only when deterministic descent, scale, and out-of-distribution safeguards pass; otherwise retain deterministic recovery.
Train on existing optimization-trajectory data without additional function or gradient evaluations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 480 CUTEst problems, all six learning-assisted variants improved robustness at broadly comparable evaluation costs; a conductivity-identification example also illustrated potential cost and runtime reductions.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits may depend on safeguard and prediction-trigger settings, and the abstract does not establish performance guarantees beyond the tested problems.
infographic.paper_title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods

title: Compact MaxSAT Encodings for Balanced Waiting in B2B Meeting Scheduling
authors: Tuyen Van Kieu, Long Duc Nguyen, Minh Duc Dang Vu, Khanh Van To
abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) meeting schedules can leave participants with long and uneven waits. Earlier break-based B2B models count interruptions without measuring their duration. Our earlier work minimizes the range of participant idle totals, but a minimum range can still leave long waits. We study lexicographic optimization of idle range, maximum idle, and total idle, in that order. Waiting is measured in empty slots between a participant's first and last meetings. Balance compares idle totals among participants requesting at least two meetings. Using weighted maximum satisfiability (MaxSAT), we prove preservation of feasible schedules, objective costs, and priorities. Compact-Base retains our earlier feasibility encoding; Compact-Objective adds objective-specific representations. We compare both with Direct, an independent implementation based on the 2022 MaxSAT model. Encoding comparisons use three repetitions per encoding-objective-instance combination on 226 variants of 20 base instances. Schedule-quality comparisons use break, range, and lexicographic objectives with the same encoding and feasible set. Across nine objective-dataset comparisons, Compact-Objective had the lowest median clause count and lower median peak memory than Direct. Runtime rankings changed in comparisons with the same solver build and computing environment. On 84 instances solved optimally under all three quality objectives, selected lexicographic schedules preserved the optimal idle range. Compared with selected range-only schedules, maximum idle decreased on 11 instances and total idle on 56. On 68 instances also solved optimally under range-then-total optimization, the selected schedules matched the three-tier criterion values. Compact-Base supplied the larger clause reduction relative to Direct; Compact-Objective reduced clauses further.

infographic.key_insight: Lexicographically minimizing idle range, maximum idle, then total idle can reduce waiting while preserving optimal balance in B2B meeting schedules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact MaxSAT encodings offer a lower-memory approach to balanced meeting scheduling, though fewer clauses do not consistently imply faster solving.
method: Measure waiting as empty slots between each participant’s first and last meetings.
Optimize idle range, maximum idle, and total idle in strict priority order.
Compare Direct, Compact-Base, and Compact-Objective encodings with proven preservation of feasibility, costs, and priorities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests covered 226 variants of 20 base instances with three repetitions per configuration; among 84 instances optimal under all three quality objectives, selected lexicographic schedules preserved optimal range and reduced maximum idle on 11 and total idle on 56 versus selected range-only schedules.
infographic.watch_item: Runtime rankings varied, so benchmark the encodings on target workloads rather than treating clause reductions as guaranteed speedups.
infographic.paper_title: Compact MaxSAT Encodings for Balanced Waiting in B2B Meeting Scheduling

title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
authors: Yin Liu, Shanshan Zhao, Didong Li
abstract: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

infographic.key_insight: TSGSurv connects faithful generation of censored time-to-event data to consistent Cox model estimates, while showing that valid inference requires more than distributional fidelity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports synthetic survival data for biomedical data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twins, with corrections for downstream statistical inference.
method: Use a two-stage framework to jointly generate observed times and covariates conditional on event status.
Establish distributional convergence rates and conditions for consistent Cox coefficient estimates.
Apply variance correction and distribution calibration to recover valid inference for the original data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive simulations and two real-data applications, but provides no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Naive inference from synthetic data can be unreliable; consistency depends on stated conditions, and valid inference requires the proposed corrections.
infographic.paper_title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference

title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
authors: Francesco Caporali, Jason M. Altschuler, Boris Hanin
abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{λ_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes adapt gradient descent to local curvature, promoting convergence toward flatter interpolating minima.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CDP offers an adaptive stepsize approach with a SAM-like flattening effect, including in reported experiments on pre-trained LLM fine-tuning.
method: Multiply the classical Polyak stepsize by 4 and a mild damping factor.
Use critical equioscillations near the minimizer manifold while damping drives convergence.
At small loss, projected iterates approximately descend log maximum Hessian eigenvalue along the minimizer manifold.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports uniform-in-time sharpness and loss-reduction guarantees for locally quadratic Morse–Bott losses, plus flattening experiments on nonlinear teacher–student networks and LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require local Morse–Bott structure; empirical flattening beyond this regime does not establish the same convergence guarantees.
infographic.paper_title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
